title: The cranes and the Pygmies
greek: γέρανοι (geranoi), cranes; Πυγμαῖοι (Pygmaioi), Pygmies
short: The Trojans advance shrieking like migrating cranes, which in Greek legend fly south each winter to make war on the Pygmies at the edge of the world.
body: Book III opens by contrasting the two armies through sound. The Trojans come on with clamour (κλαγγή, the harsh cry of birds) like cranes escaping the northern winter and flying to 'the streams of Ocean', the river that rings the earth, where they bring 'slaughter and death to Pigmy men'. This is the earliest mention of the Pygmies (Πυγμαῖοι, 'fist-high men', from πυγμή, fist, also a short measure of length) and of their war with the cranes, a story much loved by later poets and vase-painters. Aristotle insisted that it was no fable and placed the little people in the marshes near the sources of the Nile (History of Animals 8.12, 597a); Leaf suggests that reports of African peoples may have reached early Greece along with the ivory trade. Virgil reworks the simile for the shouting Trojans of Aeneid 10.264-6. Against the noisy Trojans the Achaeans advance 'in silence, breathing fury' (3.8), a contrast the poet develops again in the paired similes of 4.422-38.

title: The mist on the mountain (simile)
greek: Νότος (Notos), the South Wind; ὀμίχλη (omichlē), mist
short: The dust raised by the marching armies is compared to a mountain mist brought by the South Wind: hated by the shepherd, 'better than night' for the thief.
body: The second simile of the book turns from sound to sight. The South Wind (Νότος), the damp wind of the Greek winter, pours mist over the peaks so thickly that a man can see only 'so far as he casteth a stone'. The comparison is built round two opposed human viewpoints: the shepherd, who loses sight of his flock, hates such weather, while the robber welcomes it as 'better than night'. The literal point of comparison is the dust-cloud (κονίσαλος) raised by thousands of feet, but the figure of the thief quietly colours the advance with menace. Leaf notes that the simile is introduced by εὖτε in the unusual sense 'like as', paralleled only at 19.386; ancient critics who took it as 'when' had to make line 12 the main clause, a construction without parallel in Homeric similes. Like the goatherd and shepherd similes of Book IV (4.275-9, 4.452-5), this one translates the movement of armies into a scene from ordinary country life.

title: Alexander (Paris)
greek: Ἀλέξανδρος (Alexandros); Πάρις (Paris); θεοειδής (theoeidēs), godlike in appearance
short: Helen's lover is usually called Alexander (Alexandros) in the Iliad; Book III shows him as a handsome, showily armed champion who cannot face his challenge.
body: The Trojan prince has two names. Homer uses both names; Alexandros is the usual name in narration and in the mouths of most speakers, while Paris is the form Hector uses, often in rebuke, as in 'Evil Paris' (3.39). Alexandros is good Greek ('defender of men', from ἀλέξω, ward off, and ἀνήρ, man); Apollodorus says the exposed child, raised among herdsmen, earned it by beating off robbers from the flocks (Library 3.12.5). A Hittite treaty of about 1280 BC names Alaksandu, king of Wilusa, a place most scholars equate with (W)ilios, Troy; the Greek-looking name is suggestive, but identifying him with Homer's Paris is speculation. His entrance here characterises him: he steps out as a front-line champion (προμάχιζεν) wearing a leopard skin and carrying a curved bow, a sword and two spears, an odd mixture for a man challenging 'all the best of the Argives' to fight. Aristarchus rejected lines 19-20 because a man dressed as an archer would not challenge heavy-armed warriors; Leaf answers that the same objection would apply to προμάχιζεν, and that Paris carries the archer's skin and bow and the spearman's pair of spears together. One sight of Menelaus sends him back into the ranks. The epithet 'godlike' (θεοειδής, 'god-like in form') is pointed: his looks are his chief claim.

title: Menelaus as a hungry lion
greek: λέων (leōn), lion; ἐχάρη (echarē), he rejoiced
short: Menelaus sees Paris and rejoices like a hungry lion that comes upon a fresh carcass: the simile captures his appetite for revenge.
body: Menelaus, whose stock epithet 'dear to Ares' (ἀρηΐφιλος) marks him as a warrior, is compared to a hungry lion that lights on the body of a stag or wild goat and devours it even while dogs and young hunters rush at him. Lion similes are the commonest animal similes in the Iliad and regularly mark a fighter's aggression. Leaf explains the scene as a lion seizing game just killed by a hunting party, under the hunters' eyes. Some ancient critics objected that a lion does not eat what it has not killed and took σῶμα as a living animal, but Aristarchus rightly answered that Homer never uses σῶμα of a living body. The point of the simile is Menelaus's joy (ἐχάρη): he thinks he can now punish the 'sinner' (ἀλείτην, 3.28). The next simile reverses the mood, as Paris recoils like a man who has come on a snake. The paired similes forecast the duel: the wronged husband eager, the seducer afraid.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.23

title: Paris and the snake (simile)
greek: δράκων (drakōn), snake; παλίνορσος (palinorsos), starting back
short: Paris shrinks from Menelaus like a man who starts back, trembling and pale, from a snake in a mountain glen.
body: This simile follows directly on the lion simile and inverts it: Menelaus is the predator, Paris the startled passer-by. The physical signs of fear are listed one after another: the man starts back (παλίνορσος, a word found only here in Homer), trembling seizes his limbs, and pallor (ὦχρος) takes his cheeks. Leaf notes that Virgil copied the simile for the Greek Androgeos, who realises too late that he has walked into a band of Trojans and recoils 'like a man who has trodden on an unseen snake among rough briars' (Aeneid 2.379-81). In Homer the image prepares for Hector's scornful speech that follows: the champion who strode out in a leopard skin is now a frightened traveller. The contrast of the two similes is a good example of how Homer uses comparisons in pairs to present one encounter from both sides.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.33
Virgil, Aeneid 2.379-82 (Latin text, ed. Greenough, on Scaife/Perseus)

title: Dysparis, 'Evil Paris': Hector's rebuke
greek: Δύσπαρι (Dyspari), vocative of Δύσπαρις, 'ill-starred Paris'
short: Hector's insult 'Dysparis', 'Evil Paris', opens a famous rebuke that sums up how Troy sees the man who caused its war.
body: Hector's speech begins with a compound coined from his brother's name, Δύσπαρι, with the prefix δυσ- ('bad, ill-'): 'Paris-gone-wrong'. Leaf compares Telemachus's 'mother, un-mother' (μῆτερ δύσμητερ, Od. 23.97), Euripides' 'Dys-Helen' and 'Ainoparis', and a line of the Spartan poet Alcman, 'Dysparis, Ainoparis, a bane to Greece'. The rest of the line piles up abuse: 'most fair to look upon' (εἶδος ἄριστε), 'mad after women' (γυναιμανές), 'beguiler' (ἠπεροπευτά). Hector wishes Paris had never been born or had died unwed, says he is a reproach to father, city and people, and mocks his lyre, hair and looks as 'gifts of Aphrodite' that will not help him 'in the dust'. The scene sets a pattern for the brothers: Hector rebukes Paris again at 6.325-31 and 13.769-73, where the same opening words recur, and Paris answers mildly each time.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.39
Homer, Odyssey 23.97 (Greek text, ed. Monro and Allen, on Scaife/Perseus)

title: 'A coat of stone' (death by stoning)
greek: λάϊνον ἕσσο χιτῶνα (laïnon hesso chitōna), you would have put on a tunic of stone
short: A grim joke: if the Trojans were not cowards, Paris would long ago have 'put on a tunic of stone', that is, been stoned to death.
body: Hector's phrase is a metaphor for public execution by stoning: the heap of stones that kills the condemned man covers him like a garment and becomes his grave. Leaf compares the chorus of Sophocles' Ajax, who fear death by stoning (λιθόλευστον Ἄρη, Aj. 253-4), and notes that later poets use the parallel image of 'clothing oneself in earth' as a euphemism for burial (Pindar, Nemean 11.16). Aeschylus' Clytemnestra makes a similar grim joke: had Agamemnon died as often as rumour claimed, he would have needed a 'cloak of earth' for each body (Agamemnon 870-3). Stoning was a communal punishment for someone who had harmed the whole people, so the line hints that Paris is regarded in Troy as a public offender. It prepares for the end of the book, where the narrator says the Trojans hated him 'even as black death' (3.454).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.57

title: The gifts of the gods (Paris's reply)
greek: θεῶν ἐρικυδέα δῶρα (theōn erikudea dōra), the glorious gifts of the gods
short: Paris answers Hector with grace: the gods' gifts, beauty included, can neither be refused nor won by effort.
body: Paris first concedes that Hector's rebuke is just ('duly, and not beyond what is due', κατ' αἶσαν οὐδ' ὑπὲρ αἶσαν). He then likens his brother's heart to an axe that a shipwright drives through a beam, an unwearying tool that multiplies the force of the blow (3.60-3): a compliment that is also a gentle criticism of an inflexible temper. Then he defends beauty: 'Not to be flung aside are the glorious gifts of the gods, even all that of themselves they give, whereas by his own will could no man win them' (3.65-6). The thought that gods hand out qualities and fortunes that mortals can neither choose nor reject runs through the poem and receives its fullest statement in Achilles' parable of the two jars of Zeus (24.527-33). From Paris it is also self-serving, an excuse for the pleasures that began the war. 'Golden' (χρυσέη) is Aphrodite's regular epithet; Leaf discusses its scansion here. Paris then proposes the single combat for Helen and her possessions.

title: Horkia: 'cutting' the oaths
greek: ὅρκια πιστὰ τάμνειν (horkia pista temnein), to cut trusty oath-offerings
short: Murray's 'oaths of faith with sacrifice' renders horkia pista, oath-victims 'cut' to seal a treaty; the plot of Books III-IV turns on them.
body: The Greek behind 'swear friendship and oaths of faith with sacrifice' is φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες, literally 'cutting friendship and trusty oath-offerings'. ὅρκια are the sacrificial victims of an oath and, by extension, the treaty they seal (LSJ); 'to cut horkia' preserves the memory of the slaughter that made the agreement binding, much as Latin speaks of 'striking' a treaty (foedus ferire). Leaf notes that by Homer's time the phrase is partly metaphorical: Menelaus asks for Priam to come 'that he may cut the oaths' (3.105), yet the actual killing is done by Agamemnon. The oath of 3.264-301 is the most elaborate in Homer, and its violation by Pandarus in Book IV, an episode the ancients called 'The Breaking of the Oaths' (Aelian, Varia Historia 13.14), gives the Achaeans the moral right to destroy Troy, as Agamemnon insists at 4.155-68 and 4.234-9.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.105

anchor: white ram and a black ewe
title: The three lambs for Earth, Sun and Zeus
greek: ἄρν' ἕτερον λευκόν, ἑτέρην δὲ μέλαιναν (arn' heteron leukon, heterēn de melainan)
short: Menelaus asks for a white male lamb and a black female one for the Sun and Earth, and a third for Zeus: colours matched to the powers invoked.
body: Murray's order, 'a white ram and a black ewe, for Earth and Sun', follows the Greek word order (Γῇ τε καὶ Ἠελίῳ), but the sense is crossed: the white male is for the Sun, the black female for Earth. Greek sacrifice normally matched victims to their recipients, pale animals for the gods of the sky, dark ones for the powers of earth and the dead; compare the black ram and ewe Odysseus offers to the ghosts (Od. 10.524-7). The Achaeans will bring a third lamb for Zeus, guardian of oaths. Leaf suspected line 104 on linguistic grounds (the late form γῆ) and because only Trojan lambs appear in the ritual that follows; without it, he suggests, the white lamb would be for the heavenly gods and the black for the gods below (3.276-9), though he admits that a male and a female victim suit a male and a female deity. Menelaus also insists on Priam's presence because Priam's sons are 'over-weening and faithless' (3.106), an ominous forecast of what Pandarus will do.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.104

title: Helen's web
greek: μέγαν ἱστὸν ... δίπλακα πορφυρέην (megan histon ... diplaka porphyreēn), a great purple web of double fold
short: Helen's first appearance: she is weaving a purple cloth that pictures the battles fought for her sake, an image often read as a figure for the poem itself.
body: Helen enters the Iliad at her loom, weaving a large purple cloth 'of double fold' (δίπλαξ, big enough to be worn doubled) into which she works 'many contests' (ἀέθλους) of Trojans and Achaeans 'that for her sake they had endured at the hands of Ares'. Leaf takes the passage as evidence that pictorial weaving was highly developed, perhaps by inserting coloured threads by hand, and compares the Bayeux Tapestry. Critics have read the web as a figure for epic song: Helen is the one character who makes a record of the war while it is happening, and she places herself at its cause. Ann Bergren argued that the 'tableau' quality of Book III, which replays the war's beginning in its tenth year, belongs to the special time of Helen's web. Compare Andromache, who is weaving flowers, not war, when Hector dies (22.440-1), and Helen's own words that Zeus gave her and Paris an evil fate 'that hereafter we may be a song for men to come' (6.357-8).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.126

title: Aethra, daughter of Pittheus
greek: Αἴθρη Πιτθῆος θυγάτηρ (Aithrē Pitthēos thugatēr)
short: One of Helen's maids is Aethra, daughter of Pittheus, in later myth the mother of Theseus; ancient and modern critics suspected the line.
body: In later legend Aethra (Αἴθρη), daughter of Pittheus of Troezen, was the mother of the Athenian hero Theseus. When Theseus carried off the young Helen, her brothers Castor and Polydeuces rescued her and took Aethra captive as her slave; at the sack of Troy Aethra's grandsons Demophon and Acamas found her among Helen's servants and took her home. Leaf collects the evidence: the story was told in the Sack of Troy ascribed to Lesches, shown on the Chest of Cypselus with an inscription naming 'Aethra dragged from Athens', and painted by Polygnotus at Delphi (Pausanias 5.19 and 10.25). He judges line 144 an interpolation: Homer knows nothing of the Theseus legends, rarely names handmaids, and gives the epithet 'ox-eyed' (βοῶπις) almost only to Hera. The Alexandrian scholia already found it implausible that so ancient a woman should still be Helen's attendant.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.144
Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.25-26 (Polygnotus' painting of the Sack of Troy at Delphi), trans. W. H. S. Jones (Loeb)

title: The Scaean Gates
greek: Σκαιαὶ πύλαι (Skaiai pulai); σκαιός (skaios), left, western
short: The Scaean ('Left' or 'Western') Gate faces the plain and the battlefield; several of the poem's key scenes take place there.
body: Σκαιαὶ πύλαι are the gates above which the Trojan elders sit to watch the plain. σκαιός means 'left', and since Greek augurs faced north when watching for omens it also came to mean 'western' and 'ill-omened' (LSJ); which sense lies behind the name is uncertain. Whatever its origin, the gate is the poem's threshold between the city and the war. Here Hector parts from Andromache (6.392-3); here he waits alone for Achilles (22.5-6); and here the dying Hector foretells that Paris and Apollo will kill Achilles 'at the Scaean gates' (22.359-60). Book III gives the gate its first role: the old men of Troy, past fighting, sit 'upon the wall' (ἐπὶ πύργῳ) beside it, and Helen comes to them there.

sources.cite: Liddell, Scott and Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed., Oxford 1940), s.v. σκαιός

Homer, Iliad 6.392-3 (Greek text, ed. Monro and Allen, Oxford 1920, on Scaife/Perseus)

title: The Trojan elders as cicadas
greek: τέττιγες (tettiges), cicadas; ὄπα λειριόεσσαν (opa leirioessan), 'lily-like' voice
short: The aged counsellors on the wall, too old to fight but still fine speakers, are compared to cicadas chirping in a tree.
body: The elders (δημογέροντες) include Priam's brothers Lampus, Clytius and Hicetaon (sons of Laomedon, as 20.237-8 shows) and the counsellors Ucalegon and Antenor. Too old for battle, they are 'speakers full good', and Homer compares them to cicadas (τέττιγες) perched in a tree, pouring out their 'lily-like voice'. The simile is affectionate and faintly comic: Greeks loved the cicada's song, and the old men's thin, unending talk resembles it. Leaf confesses that no one knows exactly how a voice can be 'lily-like'; the scholia gloss the word as 'delightful, sweet', and Hesiod uses it of the Muses' voice (Theogony 41). One elder became famous through Virgil: as Troy burns, 'already Ucalegon's house next door is ablaze' (Aeneid 2.311-12), and Juvenal borrows the name for a neighbour moving out in a fire (Satires 3.198-9). The name itself looks like οὐκ ἀλέγων, 'not caring'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.152
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.146

title: 'Small blame': Helen's beauty seen through its effect
greek: οὐ νέμεσις (ou nemesis), there is no cause for indignation
short: Seeing Helen, the old men concede that her beauty justifies the long war, yet still want her sent away: beauty shown through its effect, not described.
body: οὐ νέμεσις means 'there is no ground for indignation' (νέμεσις is righteous resentment at what is improper); Leaf, like Murray, renders it 'Small blame that'. The elders whisper that Trojans and Achaeans cannot be blamed for suffering so long 'for such a woman', since 'wondrously like is she to the immortal goddesses to look upon'; nevertheless she should sail home before she becomes a bane to their children. Homer never describes Helen's face. Lessing, in chapter 21 of Laocoön (1766), made this passage his chief example of how poetry should render beauty: not by listing features, which painting does better, but by showing its effect, here on cold old men who of all people should resist it. The double verdict, sympathy and rejection, sums up Troy's attitude to Helen and contrasts with Priam's gentleness in the speech that follows.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.156
G. E. Lessing, Laocoön: An Essay on the Limits of Painting and Poetry (1766), ch. 21 (English trans. on Project Gutenberg)

anchor: nowise to blame in my eyes
title: 'The gods are to blame': Priam and Helen
greek: οὔ τί μοι αἰτίη ἐσσί, θεοί νύ μοι αἴτιοί εἰσιν (ou ti moi aitiē essi, theoi nu moi aitioi eisin)
short: Priam tells Helen he does not blame her; the gods are responsible for the war. The poem keeps testing this idea of divine responsibility.
body: Priam's kindness to his daughter-in-law is one of the most humane moments in the poem: 'thou art nowise to blame (αἰτίη) in my eyes; it is the gods, methinks, that are to blame'. It also states a recurring Homeric way of explaining disaster. Events are regularly given both a human and a divine cause, and characters can stress either. Agamemnon uses the same language to excuse himself to Achilles: 'I am not to blame (αἴτιος), but Zeus and Fate and the Erinys' (19.86-7), a passage E. R. Dodds made the starting point of his study of Homeric psychology. In the Odyssey Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for troubles they bring on themselves 'beyond their lot' (Od. 1.32-4). Helen takes the opposite view of her own case and blames herself bitterly ('shameless me', 3.180; compare 6.344-58). The poem lets the two perspectives stand side by side.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 19.86-7 (Greek text, ed. Monro and Allen, Oxford 1920, on Scaife/Perseus)
E. R. Dodds, The Greeks and the Irrational (Berkeley 1951), ch. 1, 'Agamemnon's Apology'

title: The View from the Wall (Teichoskopia)
greek: τειχοσκοπία (teichoskopia), viewing from the wall
short: Priam asks Helen to name the Greek leaders: the 'View from the Wall', a scene that logically belongs to the first year of the war, not the tenth.
body: From 3.161 to 3.244 Helen identifies Agamemnon, Odysseus, Aias and Idomeneus for Priam, with Antenor adding his memories of Odysseus and Menelaus. The episode is known as the Teichoskopia, and the term is now used for any such scene (Euripides imitates it in Phoenissae 88-201). Readers have long noticed that it is strange for Priam not to know the enemy commanders after nine years of siege. The usual explanation is that the poet deliberately re-stages the beginning of the war: the duel to settle the quarrel, the treaty, the introduction of the chief heroes and the reminder of Helen's abduction all belong to a beginning and give the audience what it needs. Leaf, Kirk and others treated the scene as a digression inserted into the story of the duel; N. Postlethwaite (1985) and the Basel commentary on Book III discuss how it works within the book. Each of Helen's descriptions turns back to her own guilt and lost family.

sources.cite: N. Postlethwaite, 'The Duel of Paris and Menelaos and the Teichoskopia in Iliad 3', Antichthon 19 (1985) 1-6
M. Krieter-Spiro, Homer's Iliad: The Basel Commentary, Book III, ed. S. D. Olson, trans. B. W. Millis and S. Strack (Berlin and Boston: De Gruyter, 2015)

title: Kynōpis, 'dog-eyed': Helen's self-reproach
greek: κυνῶπις (kunōpis), dog-eyed, shameless
short: Helen calls herself kynōpis, 'dog-eyed', that is, 'shameless': the harshest word used of her in the poem comes from her own mouth.
body: The Greek is κυνῶπις, literally 'dog-faced' or 'dog-eyed'. In Homer the dog is a byword for shamelessness and lack of restraint, so the word means 'shameless one' (LSJ); it is also used of Hera (18.396). Achilles throws the masculine form at Agamemnon (κυνῶπα, 1.159), and Hephaestus uses it of the adulterous Aphrodite (Od. 8.319). Helen applies it to herself here and again in the Odyssey (Od. 4.145), and to Hector she calls herself 'a dog, a contriver of evil' (6.344, 356). Her self-accusation balances Priam's refusal to blame her. Her wish that 'evil death had been my pleasure' when she followed Paris, and her final phrase about Agamemnon, 'husband's brother to shameless me, as sure as ever such a one there was' (εἴ ποτ' ἔην γε, literally 'if ever he was'), convey how unreal her old life now seems; Leaf discusses this much-debated idiom, which recurs at 11.762 and 24.426.

sources.cite: Liddell, Scott and Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed., Oxford 1940), s.v. κυνώπης (fem. κυνῶπις)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.180

anchor: Amazons came, the peers of men
title: Priam, the Phrygians and the Amazons
greek: Ἀμαζόνες ἀντιάνειραι (Amazones antianeirai), Amazons, a match for men
short: Priam recalls fighting as a young ally of the Phrygians against the Amazons, 'the peers of men', to measure Agamemnon's huge army.
body: Priam calls Agamemnon 'blest of heaven' (ὀλβιοδαίμων) and remembers the largest army he ever saw: the Phrygians of Otreus and Mygdon camped by the river Sangarius in north-west Anatolia, whom he joined as an ally 'on the day when the Amazons came'. Even they were fewer than the Achaeans. The Amazons are ἀντιάνειραι, 'a match for men' (literally 'equal to men'); the same epithet is used when Bellerophon kills them in Lycia (6.186), their only other mention in the Iliad (Leaf). Leaf also notes that ἐλέχθην in 3.188 may mean either 'I was numbered among them' or 'I bivouacked among them'. In the epic tradition after Homer the Amazon queen Penthesilea came to help Troy after Hector's death and was killed by Achilles, as Proclus' summary of the lost Aethiopis records. Old men recalling the wars of their youth to set the present in perspective is a Homeric pattern: compare Nestor at 1.260-72 and 4.318-25.

title: Odysseus as the ram of the flock
greek: κτίλος (ktilos), the leading ram; ἀρνειὸς πηγεσίμαλλος (arneios pēgesimallos), thick-fleeced ram
short: Priam likens Odysseus, shorter than Agamemnon but broad in shoulder and chest, to a thick-fleeced ram leading a flock of white ewes.
body: Priam sees a man 'shorter by a head than Agamemnon, but broader of shoulder and of chest' who moves among the ranks like a κτίλος, the ram that leads the flock (Leaf: 'bell-wether'). The comparison suits a leader who keeps order among the troops, and it has an aptness the Iliad's audience may have relished: in the Odyssey Odysseus escapes the Cyclops' cave clinging beneath the fleece of the biggest ram of the flock (Od. 9.431-61). Leaf notes that the image of the ram leading the flock recurs at full length at 13.492-3. The pastoral imagery fits the Homeric idea of a king as 'shepherd of the people' (ποιμὴν λαῶν). Helen's answer gives Odysseus his chief epithet, πολύμητις, 'of many wiles', and his homeland, rugged Ithaca.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.196
Homer, Odyssey 9.431-61 (Greek text, ed. Monro and Allen, on Scaife/Perseus)

title: The embassy of Odysseus and Menelaus; Antenor
greek: ἀγγελίη (angeliē), message, embassy; ἐξείνισσα (exeinissa), I entertained as guests
short: Antenor recalls the early embassy of Odysseus and Menelaus to demand Helen, when he entertained them as guests: an episode from the Cypria.
body: At the very start of the war Odysseus and Menelaus came to Troy to ask for the return of Helen and her property; the episode was narrated in the lost Cypria, where, according to Proclus' summary, the envoys were sent just after the Greeks landed and took up their first dead; Leaf, following Aristarchus, prefers to take ἀγγελίης here as 'an envoy concerning thee'. Later in the Iliad we learn that the Trojan Antimachus, bribed by Paris, urged that Menelaus be killed while on that embassy (11.138-42). Antenor instead received the envoys as guests (ἐξείνισσα), the language of xenia, the guest-friendship that bound host and guest and their families. Antenor is Troy's voice of moderation: in 7.347-53 he proposes giving Helen back. Later tradition remembered him as spared by the Greeks, or even as a traitor, and Virgil makes him the founder of Patavium (Padua) in Italy (Aeneid 1.242-9). His memory introduces the sketch of the two envoys' contrasting ways of speaking.

title: Odysseus' eloquence: 'words like snowflakes'
greek: ἔπεα νιφάδεσσιν ἐοικότα χειμερίῃσιν (epea niphadessin eoikota cheimeriēisin)
short: Antenor contrasts Menelaus' brief, clear speech with Odysseus' awkward start and overwhelming flood of words 'like snowflakes on a winter's day'.
body: Menelaus spoke 'fluently, with few words, but very clearly' (παῦρα μέν, ἀλλὰ μάλα λιγέως). Odysseus would stand with eyes fixed on the ground, holding his staff stiff, so that he seemed sullen or a fool; but once his great voice came from his chest with 'words like snowflakes on a winter's day', no mortal could rival him. The snow image suggests density, abundance and an irresistible covering. Ancient rhetoricians read the passage, together with Nestor's 'sweeter than honey' speech (1.249), as Homer's demonstration of three styles of oratory: Quintilian assigns the plain, concise style to Menelaus, the sweet middle style to Nestor, and the grand, vehement style to Odysseus (Institutio Oratoria 12.10.64). The deceptively unimpressive Odysseus who then overwhelms his audience anticipates the beggar-Odysseus of the Odyssey.

title: Aias, 'bulwark of the Achaeans'
greek: πελώριος ἕρκος Ἀχαιῶν (pelōrios herkos Achaiōn), huge, the wall of the Achaeans
short: Aias, son of Telamon, is 'huge' and 'the bulwark (herkos) of the Achaeans', the army's defensive wall, a role he plays above all in Books XI-XVII.
body: ἕρκος means a fence, enclosure or wall (LSJ), and Aias of Salamis, the son of Telamon, is the Achaeans' living wall, the defensive hero who carries a body-length shield 'like a tower' (7.219) and holds the line when Hector storms the ships (Book XV). Nestor uses the same phrase of Achilles at 1.284. The word recurs in Book IV in other senses: the taslet is 'a barrier against darts' (4.137), Nestor's infantry is 'a bulwark of battle' (4.299), and Odysseus speaks of 'the barrier of thy teeth' (4.350). Leaf finds it remarkable that Aias is dismissed in one line and Diomedes not mentioned at all, while Idomeneus receives fuller treatment; he suspected that Idomeneus here displaces more famous warriors.

title: Castor and Polydeuces: 'the life-giving earth held them'
greek: φυσίζοος αἶα (phusizoos aia), the life-giving earth
short: Helen wonders why her brothers are missing; the narrator tells us they are already dead and buried, held by the 'life-giving earth' of their homeland.
body: Helen looks for her twin brothers, Castor 'tamer of horses' and Polydeuces 'the goodly boxer', and imagines that they stay away for shame at her disgrace. The narrator then tells us what she does not know: 'the life-giving earth held them fast there in Lacedaemon, in their dear native land.' Leaf notes how the conventional epithet φυσίζοος, 'life-producing', seems to modern taste inappropriate in a statement of death. Ruskin admired exactly that: the poet 'has to speak of the earth in sadness' but refuses to let his feeling alter the fact that the earth is still fruitful and life-giving, the opposite of the 'pathetic fallacy' (Modern Painters III, ch. 12, §12). The Iliad treats the twins as mortal; the Odyssey (11.300-4) knows the later story that they share immortality on alternate days. Their death was narrated in the Cypria (Leaf), where, according to Proclus' summary, Castor was killed fighting Idas and Lynceus.

anchor: cut hair from off the heads
title: The oath ritual
greek: ἀρνῶν ἐκ κεφαλέων τάμνε τρίχας (arnōn ek kephaleōn tamne trichas), he cut hair from the lambs' heads
short: The oath ceremony: wine is mixed, the kings' hands washed, and hair cut from the victims' heads is shared among the leaders so that all take part.
body: The sequence is carefully described. The heralds bring the victims and mix the wine in a bowl; water is poured over the kings' hands; Agamemnon draws the knife that hangs beside his sword-sheath and cuts hair from the lambs' heads, which the heralds share among the leaders of both sides. Cutting the victim's hair is the opening act of ordinary sacrifice too (Od. 14.422), where it is thrown into the fire; Leaf explains it as a first portion standing for the whole victim, not burnt here because no fire is used in an oath-sacrifice, and shared out so that every chieftain takes part in the sacrifice and its curse. Then come Agamemnon's prayer, the cutting of the lambs' throats, and the libation with its curse (3.276-301). The victims of an oath are not eaten: Priam takes his lambs back to Troy (3.310), and in Book XIX the boar sacrificed at the reconciliation of Agamemnon and Achilles is thrown into the sea (19.266-8). A scholion says native victims were buried and foreign ones thrown into the sea; Leaf suspects this is a deduction from these two passages. Agamemnon recalls each element when the oath is broken (4.158-9).

anchor: ye that in the world below
title: The divine witnesses of the oath
greek: Ζεῦ πάτερ Ἴδηθεν μεδέων (Zeu pater Idēthen medeōn); οἳ ὑπένερθε καμόντας ἀνθρώπους τίνυσθον (hoi hupenerthe kamontas anthrōpous tinusthon)
short: Agamemnon calls to witness Zeus who rules from Ida, the all-seeing Sun, the rivers, Earth, and the powers below who punish perjurers after death.
body: Each witness has a reason. Zeus is invoked as 'ruling from Ida' (Ἴδηθεν μεδέων), the mountain above Troy where he has a precinct and altar (8.47-8); Leaf observes that he is named as the god of Ida, and the Rivers, as local divinities, are included because the Trojans are a party to the oath. The Sun, 'that beholdest all things and hearest all things', is the natural witness of what men do. Finally come 'ye that in the world below take vengeance on men that are done with life (καμόντας), whosoever hath sworn a false oath'. Leaf takes them to be Hades and Persephone, whereas the parallel oath in Book XIX names the Erinyes, 'who under the earth take vengeance on men' (19.259-60). He also records the old argument that punishment after death is otherwise almost foreign to Homer's underworld, which makes these two oaths unusual.

anchor: their brains be thus poured forth
title: The libation curse
greek: ὧδέ σφ' ἐγκέφαλος χαμάδις ῥέοι ὡς ὅδε οἶνος (hōde sph' enkephalos chamadis rheoi hōs hode oinos)
short: As the wine is poured on the ground, both armies pray that oath-breakers' brains may be spilled in the same way: a curse acted out.
body: Ordinarily a libation is a drink offered to please the gods; here, as Leaf notes, the pouring becomes a symbolic act: 'may their brains be thus poured forth upon the ground even as this wine, theirs and their children's; and may their wives be made slaves to others.' He compares the Roman fetial oath in Livy, where the priest prays that Jupiter strike the Roman people if they break faith 'as I strike this pig' (Livy 1.24), and Hannibal's similar oath over a lamb (Livy 21.45). The curse names exactly what will happen to Troy: men killed, children destroyed, wives enslaved, as Hector foresees for Andromache in Book VI. The narrator adds at once: 'but not yet was the son of Cronos to vouchsafe them fulfillment' (3.302), an ominous half-line that looks forward to the breach in Book IV and to Troy's fall beyond the poem.

anchor: shook them in the bronze-wrought helmet
title: Casting lots in a helmet
greek: κλήρους ἐν κυνέῃ χαλκήρεϊ πάλλον (klērous en kuneēi chalkērei pallon)
short: Lots are shaken in a helmet to decide who throws first; Hector shakes it looking away, so that no one can suspect him of favouring his brother.
body: Hector and Odysseus measure out the ground for the duel, then put lots (κλῆροι, marked tokens) into a bronze helmet. Leaf points out that the shaking itself, always done by one man, comes at 3.324: 'great Hector of the flashing helm shook the helmet, looking behind him (ἂψ ὁρόων)', that is, averting his eyes so that no one could accuse him of manipulating the result; Paris's lot jumps out. The same method chooses the champion to face Hector in Book VII, where each man marks his own lot and Aias's leaps out (7.171-91). The idea of the lot also underlies Homeric thinking about fate and portion: Poseidon says the brothers Zeus, Poseidon and Hades divided the world by lot (15.187-93).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.316

title: Paris's arming scene
greek: κνημῖδας μὲν πρῶτα περὶ κνήμῃσιν ἔθηκε (knēmidas men prōta peri knēmēisin ethēke)
short: Paris's arming is the first of the Iliad's four great arming scenes, which always follow the same order: greaves, corselet, sword, shield, helmet, spear.
body: Homer has a set pattern, a 'type-scene', for a warrior putting on his armour. Leaf lists the parallels (Agamemnon 11.17ff., Patroclus 16.131ff., Achilles 19.369ff.) and notes that the six pieces always appear in the same order, the natural one except that the helmet would more naturally go on before the shield. J. I. Armstrong showed how the poet expands or varies the pattern to mark the importance of the fight to come. Here the details characterise Paris: his greaves have silver ankle-pieces, and he puts on the corselet of his brother Lycaon, perhaps because the archer of 3.17 has none of his own. The plume 'nodded terribly from above', a line repeated for later heroes. Menelaus arms 'in the self-same manner' in a single line: the poet's attention is on the more decorative of the two.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900-02), note on 3.3.330

title: Menelaus' reproach to Zeus
greek: Ζεῦ πάτερ, οὔ τις σεῖο θεῶν ὀλοώτερος ἄλλος (Zeu pater, ou tis seio theōn oloōteros allos)
short: When his sword shatters, Menelaus cries that no god is more destructive than Zeus; he had prayed to punish a guest who wronged his host.
body: Before his throw Menelaus prays that Zeus let him punish Paris 'that many a one even of men yet to be may shudder to work evil to his host, that hath shown him friendship' (3.351-4). The crime is a breach of xenia, the bond between host and guest that Zeus himself protects; in Book XIII Menelaus says that Zeus of hospitality will destroy Troy for it (13.623-7). His spear pierces Paris's shield and corselet but misses the flesh, and his sword breaks on the helmet. Hence the outburst, 'Father Zeus, than thou is no other god more baleful' (ὀλοώτερος, 'more destructive'). Mortals in Homer may speak to gods with this frankness; Leaf collects similar flashes of temper against the gods (12.164, 13.631, Od. 20.201, where the herdsman Philoetius uses the same line) and compares Achilles' 'most baneful of all gods' to Apollo (22.15). The audience knows, as Menelaus does not, that Aphrodite is about to intervene.

title: Aphrodite rescues Paris
greek: ἐξήρπαξ' Ἀφροδίτη ... ἐκάλυψε δ' ἄρ' ἠέρι πολλῇ (exērpax' Aphroditē ... ekalupse d' ar' ēeri pollēi)
short: Aphrodite breaks Paris's chin-strap, then snatches him from death 'full easily, as a goddess may' and sets him down in his perfumed bedroom.
body: As Menelaus drags Paris by the helmet, Aphrodite breaks the ox-hide strap, then snatches (ἐξήρπαξε) Paris away 'full easily, as a goddess may' (ὥς τε θεός, 'as is to be expected of a goddess', Leaf), hides him in thick mist (ἠέρι πολλῇ) and sets him down 'in his fragrant, vaulted chamber'. The rescue of a favourite by a god in a cloud or mist is a recurring Iliadic pattern: Aphrodite and then Apollo save Aeneas (5.311-18, 5.344-5), Poseidon saves him again (20.318-29), and Apollo saves Hector (20.443-4). Here the effect is deliberately jarring: in a few lines we move from the dust of a duel fought before two armies to a scented bedroom, and from war to love. The duel is left undecided in form though clearly won by Menelaus, which is the opening Zeus exploits in Book IV (4.7-19).

title: Daimoniē, 'Strange goddess': Helen defies Aphrodite
greek: δαιμονίη (daimoniē), vocative of δαιμόνιος, 'strange one', 'you who act as if possessed'
short: Helen rounds on Aphrodite with daimoniē, 'strange one', and refuses her, one of the boldest speeches of a mortal to a god in Homer, until the goddess threatens her.
body: In Homer δαιμόνιος occurs only in the vocative, as an address to men or women of any rank, often between husband and wife (LSJ: 'good sir', 'lady'); it is usually understood as addressing someone whose behaviour seems strange, as if under a δαίμων's influence, and according to tone it can be reproachful, ironic or tender. Zeus uses it to Hera (1.561, and Murray's 'Strange queen' at 4.31), Hector to Andromache in tenderness (6.486). Aphrodite comes disguised as an old wool-worker from Sparta, but Helen recognises her by her neck, breasts and flashing eyes. Her speech is bitter and daring: will the goddess take her on to some new favourite in Phrygia or Maeonia? Let Aphrodite go and sit by Paris herself, give up Olympus, and fuss over him 'until he make thee his wife, or haply his slave.' Aphrodite's answer, a threat to make her hated by Trojans and Achaeans alike (3.414-17), silences her at once. The scene shows both Helen's spirit and the narrow limits of her freedom.

title: Cranae, and Paris's desire
greek: νήσῳ δ' ἐν Κραναῇ (nēsōi d' en Kranaēi), on the island of Cranae ('Rocky')
short: Unashamed by defeat, Paris recalls his first night with Helen on the island of Cranae; ancient geographers disputed where the island was.
body: Paris answers Helen's scorn with a declaration of desire: never has love so 'encompassed' his mind (ἔρως φρένας ἀμφεκάλυψεν), not even when he first carried her off from Lacedaemon and lay with her on the island of Cranae. Κραναή means 'rocky', and its location was guessed at. Pausanias put it off Gytheion in the Laconian gulf, with a sanctuary of Aphrodite Migonitis ('of Union') on the shore opposite, said to have been founded by Paris (3.22.1-2); Strabo identified it with the island Helene off Attica (9.1.22); others named Cythera. Leaf calls these 'mere guesses'. The speech has a striking parallel in Book XIV, where Zeus, beguiled by Hera, says that desire has never so overcome him (14.294, 14.315-28). Book III ends with the couple in bed and Menelaus hunting through the ranks: the war's cause has been restaged in miniature.
